parts.title: Buying a cookery course as a gift
parts.context: A woman phones a cookery school to buy a gift voucher.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a cookery school to book a course as a present. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Good afternoon, Taste of Italy Cookery School, Antonio speaking.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Hello. I'd like to buy a cookery course as a gift for someone. Is it possible to pay now and let them choose the date later?

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Yes, we sell gift vouchers. Let me take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to buy a course as a gift, so 'gift' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Chloe Brennan. That's B-R-E-N-N-A-N.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Thank you, Chloe. And who is the course for?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: It's for my father. He's retiring in June, and I'd like to give him something to do with his time. He's always said he'd like to learn to cook properly.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: What a lovely idea. When is the retirement date, so we can send the voucher in time?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: His birthday is on the ninth of June, and he retires the week after. So the voucher should be here by the ninth, really.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: We can easily do that. Does he have any food allergies we should know about?

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: Yes, he's allergic to nuts, so please make sure the chef knows. Everything else is fine.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Of course. One more thing: our vouchers are valid for six months from the date of purchase, so he'll need to book before the end of the year.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: That's fine. He'll have plenty of time.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Now, shall I tell you about our courses? The first is Italian basics, which is on Saturdays. You learn to make fresh pasta and two sauces, and it costs eighty-five pounds. That includes lunch.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: That sounds good. What else do you have?

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: There's a bread-making course on Fridays. You make a large loaf and some sweet buns, and take everything home with you. That's seventy-five pounds.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: He'd like that one too, I think. Is it a full day?

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Yes, from ten until four. And on Sundays we do Thai cooking, where you make a curry and a salad. That one is ninety pounds, because the ingredients are more expensive.

script.speaker: chloe
script.text: I think the first one is the best for a complete beginner. Can I buy the voucher for Italian basics now?

script.speaker: antonio
script.text: Certainly. I'll just need your card details, and I'll post it to you today.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A river cruise through a historic city
parts.context: A guide tells passengers what they will see on a river cruise.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide on a river boat telling passengers about a cruise through a historic city. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome aboard. My name's Harry, and I'll be your guide for the next fifty minutes. Please look at the map on the back of your ticket. We're leaving the pier, on the left of the map, and we'll be travelling east along the River Calder.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: As we set off, on the north bank, you'll see the old hospital, which closed twenty years ago and is now apartments. Directly opposite, on the south bank, close to the pier, is the market, which has been held every Saturday since the twelfth century.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: A little further on, on the north bank, just before the old bridge, is the cathedral, with the tall tower. Directly opposite the cathedral, on the south bank, is the railway station, which has the largest clock in the county.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: We'll pass under the old bridge in a moment. Please keep your heads down, as it's quite low. Once we're through, on the north bank, you'll see the castle, which was built in the thirteenth century and is now a hotel.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: On the south bank, just after the bridge, is the museum, which has a wonderful collection of old boats. And at the far end of the south bank, by the last bend in the river, is the old brewery. It stopped making beer in nineteen sixty, and it's now a theatre.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Now, a few things you might like to know. The cruise lasts fifty minutes, although in the summer we sometimes add ten minutes to see the old docks. Today, however, it's a standard cruise, and we'll be back at the pier by half past eleven.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: My commentary is in English, but if you would prefer another language, you can borrow a set of headphones from the desk by the door. They offer French, German and Spanish, and they're free.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Please keep an eye on your children. Anyone under five travels free, but they must stay with an adult at all times, and life jackets are available in all sizes.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: If you'd like to take photographs, the best place is the upper deck, where there's nothing in the way. The front of the boat is crowded, and the back is wet when the engine is running.

script.speaker: guide
script.text: Finally, if we have to cancel a cruise because of strong wind, which doesn't happen often, you'll receive a full refund. Light rain won't stop us, and there's a covered area on the lower deck. So, sit back and enjoy the trip.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A report on coastal erosion
parts.context: Two geography students plan the final sections of a field-trip report.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two geography students, Maya and Luke, discussing a report on coastal erosion. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Luke, have you finished your section on the methods for our coastal erosion report?

script.speaker: luke
script.text: Nearly. I've described how we measured the cliff retreat, but I can't remember how many measuring points we used.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Twelve. Three on each of four sections of the cliff.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: Right. And we used a tape measure, not the GPS device, because the signal was weak.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: That's right. The tape was the only thing that worked well. The GPS gave a different reading every time we checked it.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: What did we find? On the first section, the cliff has retreated by about two metres since last year.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Yes, and the section by the harbour had hardly changed, because of the sea wall.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: Dr Ahmed expected the soft clay to erode fastest, and it did. But what surprised me is that most of the loss happened after the storm in February, not gradually through the year.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: I know. We should highlight that in the results section.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: For the discussion, I'd like to suggest some solutions. What about planting grass on the cliff top?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: That helps against rainwater, but it doesn't do anything against the waves. And Dr Ahmed said we shouldn't recommend a new sea wall, because it would be far too expensive for a small village.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: So what should we recommend instead?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Moving the footpath back from the edge is cheap and sensible, so I'd put that first.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: And some signs, warning people about the danger near the worst sections. The council could do that this month.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Yes. We might mention trees, but I don't think they'd help enough.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: And closing the car park would upset local businesses, so I'd leave that out.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Agreed. Now, the practical side. When's the report due?

script.speaker: luke
script.text: Friday at noon. Dr Ahmed said there would be no extensions, even if there are technical problems.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Should we include all the photographs?

script.speaker: luke
script.text: I'd use only the best six, in an appendix at the end, rather than in the main text.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Good idea. I'll upload the report on the day, but could you proofread it first? You're much better at spelling than I am.

script.speaker: luke
script.text: Of course. Send it to me on Thursday night and I'll have it back to you by the morning.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of the printing press
parts.context: A history lecture on printing from China and Korea to Gutenberg and its effects.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the printing press. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at one of the most important inventions in history: the printing press, and the way it changed the world.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Before printing, every book had to be copied by hand, usually by monks, working in a quiet room called a scriptorium. It was slow work. A scribe could take more than a year to copy a single Bible, and so books were rare and extremely expensive. Only churches, universities and very rich people owned them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Printing did not begin in Europe. In China, printing from carved wooden blocks was in use from about the eighth century. In the eleventh century, a man named Bi Sheng invented movable type, in which each character is a separate piece, made from clay. And in Korea, movable metal type was being used by thirteen seventy-seven, to print a Buddhist text, which is the oldest surviving book printed in this way.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In Europe, the key figure was Johannes Gutenberg, who worked in the German city of Mainz around fourteen fifty. Gutenberg did not invent everything from nothing. He combined several ideas. His press was adapted from the kind used for making wine, with a heavy screw that pressed paper against the inked type. He developed an oil-based ink, which stuck to metal much better than the water-based inks used by scribes. And he made his type from a metal alloy, a mixture of lead, tin and another metal called antimony, which melted easily, set hard and could be cast in large quantities.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: His most famous book was a Bible, of which about a hundred and eighty copies were printed, each with forty-two lines on a page. By fourteen hundred and ninety-nine, presses were working in more than two hundred towns across Europe.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The effects were enormous. Books became much cheaper, so more and more people learned to read. Ideas could spread faster than ever before. When Martin Luther criticised the church in fifteen seventeen, his pamphlets were printed and sold by the thousand, and that was a major reason why the Reformation spread so quickly. Printing also helped to standardise spelling and grammar, and scientists could share their results exactly, which helped science to progress. Next week we'll look at the origins of the newspaper.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
